sections.text: The CDC lists seven groups at increased risk of heat-related illness: adults aged 65 and older, infants and young children, people with chronic medical conditions, people without air conditioning, athletes, outdoor workers and pregnant people. The groups fall into two types. Some people are at risk because their bodies cope with heat less well (age, health conditions, pregnancy, certain medications). Others are at risk because of what they are doing or where they live (exercise, outdoor work, no cooling at home). Many people belong to more than one group, and risks stack.

This article summarizes CDC guidance and does not replace advice from your own clinician. If you have a medical condition or take prescription medicine, ask a clinician how hot weather affects you and what to do on a hot day.

sections.text: Medications that change how the body handles heat

The CDC's clinician guidance on heat and medications names several classes and the mechanism for each. The table repeats those entries. Only a clinician or pharmacist can say whether a specific medicine matters for a specific person.

sections.text: The CDC also lists antihistamines, stimulants, antiseizure medicines, NSAIDs and antibiotics among the classes with relevant effects. Its patient advice is to avoid stopping any medicine abruptly without a plan in place, to discuss adjustments for hot weather with a clinician, and to know when to seek medical care and which symptoms are an emergency.

Heat index values come from the heat index calculator's formula, rounded to one decimal place. The formula was built for shade and light wind, so treat indoor figures as a rough guide.

The National Weather Service describes Extreme Caution as a category in which heat stroke, cramps or exhaustion are possible. That wording is for the general public. The calculator's own documentation notes that its number does not account for age, medications, obesity or acclimatization, so a person from one of the groups above can face real risk at a lower heat index than a healthy adult would.
Practical steps the CDC gives for older adults

items: Stay in air-conditioned buildings as much as possible.
Drink more water than usual and do not wait until you are thirsty.
Check on a friend or neighbor, and have someone do the same for you.
Seek immediate medical attention for muscle cramps, headaches, nausea or vomiting.
Assuming only the old and the very young are at risk. Athletes and outdoor workers are on the CDC list because exertion and dehydration are risks in themselves.
Relying on thirst. The CDC tells older adults not to wait until they are thirsty, and it lists ACE inhibitors and ARBs with reduced thirst sensation.
Stopping a medicine on your own in hot weather. The CDC advises against abrupt changes without a plan.
Treating the heat index as a personal safety line. It is a general-public figure for shade and light wind.
Skipping a check on neighbors who live alone. Checking on others is among the CDC's own recommendations.
Expecting this article to give statistics. The CDC page cited here gives none for these groups, so none are quoted.

sections.text: If someone becomes confused, slurs speech, has a seizure or loses consciousness in the heat, OSHA's guidance is to call 911 immediately and cool the person until help arrives.

sections.heading: Check the Heat Index
sections.body: Enter the temperature and humidity at home or outdoors to see which category you are in.
